title: Junior Haridasa
html:
The Lord's Singer

While Sri Chaitanya lived in Nilachala, two sweet-voiced kirtana singers stayed by His side, and both were named Haridasa: the Senior Haridasa and the Junior. Krishnadasa Kaviraja mentions them in his list of the branches of the Chaitanya tree:

“Bada Haridasa and Chota Haridasa, two kirtana singers, stayed by Mahaprabhu's side.” (CC, Adi 10.147)

Of the Junior Haridasa — in Bengali, Chhota Haridasa — Kaviraja tells in the second chapter of the Antya-lila, where he calls him “the Lord's singer”; there too, on the Lord's lips, he is simply “Haridasa.” Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” calls him “Haridasa the Younger,” and Ishana Nagara in the “Advaita-prakasha” “the singer Sri Haridasa.” The biographies call him Chhota Haridasa, Haridasa and Sri Haridasa.1 Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” also calls him “Laghu-haridasa”: many Vaishnavas bore the name Haridasa, and words such as laghu (junior) or madhyama (middle) were added to it.

Where he came from, who his parents were and when he appeared in this world, the sources do not say; the year of his departure is not known either, and the Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math has no days for him. All we know of him belongs to the years when the Lord lived in Puri, and the chief event of his life to the last of those years.

He lived together with Govinda, the Lord's personal servant. Having told how Govinda came to Mahaprabhu, Kaviraja adds:

“The two Haridasas, the junior and the senior, both kirtana singers, and Ramai and Nandai stayed with Govinda. Together with Govinda they served the Lord.” (CC, Madhya 10.149–150)

He was a renunciant, a vairagi: this is exactly what the Lord calls him in the story told below.2 He was indifferent to worldly things and served the Lord by singing, each time choosing a kirtana suited to His mood. Mahaprabhu loved him dearly, and so all the Lord's devotees treated him with great tenderness; Svarupa Damodara would later say of him that he was dear to the Lord.

One of the biographies opens its account of him with a reflection on music. Singing, playing instruments and dancing are condemned by the shastras as unworthy of a noble person when they serve worldly enjoyment; yet the same arts are highly praised when they are offered to the Lord and awaken attraction to Him. The Junior Haridasa's service was of this kind.

Patraka

Who the two singers are in Krishna's pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells:

“The two servants who were formerly in Vrindavana, Raktaka and Patraka, now serve Gauranga: they are Haridasa the Elder and Haridasa the Younger.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 138)

By the order of the names, the Junior Haridasa is Patraka, one of Krishna's servants in Vrindavana, and the Senior is Raktaka.3

At the Ratha-yatra

At the festival of the chariots the Lord divided the devotees into seven kirtana groups. In the fourth the lead singer was Govinda Ghosha; Haridasa, Vishnudasa, Raghava and Govinda's brothers Madhava and Vasu Ghosha sang the response, and Vakreshvara danced (CC, Madhya 13.42). Whether this Haridasa was our singer Kaviraja does not specify; one of the biographies says plainly that he was, others say so with doubt or only following the English translation.4

The Rice from Madhavi-devi

In Puri, so as to be near the Lord, lived Bhagavan Acharya. He was so close to the Lord that now and then he would invite Him to an especially fine meal, and Mahaprabhu could not say no to him. Once, preparing such a meal, he called the Junior Haridasa. The “Charitamrita” relates:

“One day the Acharya invited the Lord. At home he cooked rice and made various vegetable dishes. The Lord had a singer named Chota Haridasa. The Acharya himself called him, brought him over and said, ‘Go in my name to Shikhi Mahiti's sister, ask her for one mana of white rice and bring it.’” (CC, Antya 2.101–103)

A mana was a measure of grain used in Utkala. Although the Acharya had brought much prasada from the temple of Jagannatha, he wished to cook many dishes for the Lord at home as well, and for this he needed good rice.5

Shikhi Mahiti's sister was named Madhavi-devi. Kaviraja says of her:

“She was elderly, given to austerity, and a supreme Vaishnavi. The Lord counted her among Radhika's associates. In all the world there are only three and a half such worthy persons: Svarupa Gosani, Ramananda Raya and Shikhi Mahiti are the three, and his sister is the half.” (CC, Antya 2.104–106)

Madhavi and her brothers belonged to the Lord's innermost circle.

Haridasa begged the rice from her and brought it to the Acharya, who, much pleased, cooked it with love together with the Lord's favourite dishes, and set out with them prasada from the temple, slices of ginger, and lime with salt. At midday the Lord came to the Acharya and, seeing the rice, asked:

“‘Such excellent rice! Where did you get grain like this?’ The Acharya said, ‘It was begged from Madhavi and brought here.’ The Lord said, ‘Who went and begged it?’ The Acharya named Chota Haridasa.” (CC, Antya 2.110–111)

The Acharya had not said that he went himself, and that is why the Lord asked who had brought it. Praising the rice, Mahaprabhu finished His meal.6

“Do Not Let Him Come Here”

Returning to His residence, the Lord said to Govinda, His constant servant:

“‘From today you must keep this order of Mine: do not let Chota Haridasa come here.’” (CC, Antya 2.113)

When Haridasa learned that the Lord's door was barred to him, he was deeply grieved, and no one around could understand the reason for the order.7 For three days he ate nothing.8 Then Svarupa Damodara and the other close devotees came to the Lord and asked what offence Haridasa had committed and why he was not allowed in, since he had been fasting for three days. The Lord answered:

“‘A renunciant who converses with women — I cannot bear to see his face. The senses are hard to restrain and seize their objects; even a woman made of wood steals the mind of a sage. “One should not sit in a secluded place even with one's mother, sister or daughter, for the powerful senses drag away even a learned man.” Petty souls adopt a monkey's renunciation and wander about, letting their senses graze and conversing with women.’” (CC, Antya 2.117–120)

The words about mother, sister and daughter the Lord quotes from the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” (9.19.17) and the “Manu-samhita” (2.215).9 Having said this, Mahaprabhu went into His inner rooms so that the conversation would go no further, and the devotees, seeing how stirred He was, fell silent.10

The next day they all came to the Lord again to plead for Haridasa: his offence was small, he had learned his lesson and would not do such a thing again. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” explains why the devotees could call his fault slight: in begging rice from Madhavi, Haridasa wanted only to please the Lord by his service. For a renunciant to converse with a woman is a grave fault, but it was done for the Lord's service, not for himself. The Lord answered:

“‘My mind is not under My control: it will not look upon a renunciant who converses with women. Go, all of you, to your own duties and give up this useless talk. If you speak of it again, you will not see Me here.’” (CC, Antya 2.124–125)

This is no admission of weakness but a teacher's sternness: Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya” calls it a strictness harder than a thunderbolt. The Lord, the teacher of the world, was setting an example for sannyasis to follow. Hearing such words, the devotees covered their ears with their hands and went off to their own duties, and Mahaprabhu went to perform His midday duties. His actions are very hard to understand.

Intercessor and Comforter

The next day the Vaishnavas went to Paramananda Puri, Madhavendra Puri's disciple. The Lord honoured him deeply as a guru, since he was a godbrother of Ishvara Puri, the Lord's guru, and the devotees hoped that Puri could soften the Lord. He came to Mahaprabhu; the Lord bowed to him with reverence, seated him beside Himself and asked the purpose of his visit. Puri begged Him to show grace to Haridasa.11

The Lord, displeased, replied: “Listen, Gosani: stay here with all the Vaishnavas, and give Me leave to go to Alalanatha. I will stay there alone, with only Govinda.” Alalanatha is a lonely spot some miles from Puri. Saying this, the Lord called Govinda, bowed to Puri and set off. Puri hurried to stand before Him, humbly persuaded Him to come back into the room, and said:

“‘Do whatever You wish: You are the independent Lord. Who can tell You anything? All Your dealings are for the good of the people. None of us can know Your deep heart.’” (CC, Antya 2.135–136)

So the Lord did not forgive Haridasa. And in the way the devotees turned to an elder for intercession, and in the way the Lord honoured His guru's godbrother, the biographies see a lesson in honouring the guru and all who are close to him.12

When Puri had gone home, the Vaishnavas came to Haridasa's house. Svarupa Damodara said to him:

“‘Listen, Haridasa: we all wish you well — believe this. The Lord is the independent Supreme Lord, and He has become unbending; but in time He will show you mercy, for His heart is compassionate. If you are stubborn, His stubbornness will only grow. If you bathe and eat, His anger will pass of itself.’” (CC, Antya 2.138–140)

Haridasa obeyed: he bathed and ate, and Svarupa, comforting him with the hope of seeing the Lord's feet again, went away. He who would not tolerate the slightest deviation from siddhanta always strove ardently to draw the Lord's mercy to a devotee who had stumbled for a time; so he laboured for the Junior Haridasa too.

From then on Haridasa did not show himself to the Lord: when Mahaprabhu went to the temple to see Jagannatha, he only watched Him from afar. Kaviraja writes:

“Mahaprabhu is an ocean of mercy — who can understand Him? He punishes His own devotee to make people understand dharma. Seeing this, all the devotees were struck with fear, and even in their dreams they gave up talking with women.” (CC, Antya 2.143–144)

This refers, as Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains, to sadhakas who wore the renunciant's garb. So a whole year passed, but the Lord did not relent towards Haridasa.

At the Triveni

A year later, on the anniversary of his punishment, Haridasa left Puri:

“At the end of the night he offered prostrate obeisances to the Lord and went to Prayaga without saying anything to anyone.” (CC, Antya 2.146)

There, where the Ganga meets the Yamuna and the Sarasvati, at the Triveni, Haridasa, firmly resolved to attain the Lord's feet, entered the waters and gave up his body.13 Kaviraja continues:

“At that very moment he came to the Lord in a divine body; and, having received His mercy, he remained invisible. In the body of a Gandharva he sang invisibly. At night he would let the Lord hear his songs, and no one else knew.” (CC, Antya 2.148–149)

This body is no phantom shell but a divine, non-material body given to him by the Lord's mercy, and in it he did what he had done all his life: he sang for the Lord. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that in his divine body Haridasa served the Lord invisibly with kirtana. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura, in his brief summary of the chapter, tells the story in the same way and in a few words: a year later Haridasa immersed himself in the waters of the Triveni at Prayaga and gave up his body, and then in a non-worldly body he sang for Mahaprabhu.

Haridasa's departure cannot be measured by a worldly yardstick, nor taken as a pattern to follow. It was not suicide in the worldly sense, nor the act of a man in despair: the “Charitamrita” speaks of a resolve to attain the Lord's feet; Svarupa, whose judgement the Lord always accepted, flatly rejected the guess of suicide; and the Lord Himself, as we shall see, accepted His singer's service. This is the pastime of an eternal associate, enacted by the Lord's will to teach the world, not a rule for the sadhaka.

A Voice by the Sea

One day Mahaprabhu asked the devotees, “Where is Haridasa? Bring him here.” They answered that on the anniversary of his punishment Haridasa had gone away in the night and no one knew where. Hearing this, the Lord only smiled a little, and the devotees were filled with wonder.

Another day Jagadananda, Svarupa, Govinda, Kashishvara, Shankara, Damodara and Mukunda went to bathe in the sea, and some distance away they heard Haridasa singing, as if calling out at the top of his voice. They saw no singer; they only heard his wondrous voice. And Govinda and the others began to guess: “Haridasa must have taken poison or something like it and killed himself, and by that sin, we think, he has become a brahma-rakshasa. We see no form; we only hear his song” (CC, Antya 2.155–157).14 Svarupa objected:

“‘This guess is false. From his birth he sang of Krishna and served the Lord; he was a recipient of the Lord's mercy, and he left his body in a holy place. No evil end can be his; his end is a blessed one. This is the Lord's way — later you will know it for certain.’” (CC, Antya 2.157–159)

By the holy place Svarupa means the Triveni at Prayaga.15 His judgements were always sound, and the Lord accepted them.

“A Man Reaps the Fruit of His Own Deeds”

Later a Vaishnava came from Prayaga to Navadvipa and told about Haridasa: with what resolve he had entered the Triveni and how he had carried out his purpose. Srivasa Pandita and the other devotees were amazed. The next year, as usual, the Bengali devotees led by Shivananda Sena came to the Lord in Puri, and Srivasa asked after Haridasa. Mahaprabhu answered:

“‘A man reaps the fruit of his own deeds.’” (CC, Antya 2.163)

In Bengali the Lord said this in the words of scripture: sva-karma-phala-bhuk puman, “a man enjoys the fruit of his own deeds.”

Then Srivasa told all that he had heard. The Lord smiled and, His heart well pleased, said: “For one who looks at women, this is the atonement” (CC, Antya 2.165). These are the words of the Lord as the guru of the world, Who, as Srila Bhaktisiddhanta says, is establishing a rule. Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains to whom it is addressed: to a sadhaka who wears the renunciant's garb and yet deliberately looks at women — by leaving his body at the Triveni, such a person will in future become faultless. This is not a prescription to be imitated: the Lord shows how grave such a fault is for a renunciant. And the Lord rejoiced not that Haridasa had left his body but at his destiny: by the power of the Triveni His singer had come to Him.

The devotees came to the same conclusion:

“Then Svarupa and the others came together and reflected: by the power of the Triveni, Haridasa had come to the Lord.” (CC, Antya 2.166)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta sees in this the fruit of leaving the body at the Triveni and other holy places of Vishnu; one of the biographies adds that thus the Junior Haridasa attained the position of Mahaprabhu's eternal associate.16

The Lesson

Krishnadasa Kaviraja briefly mentions this story twice more: in the summary of the Lord's pastimes — “Then the Lord punished Chota Haridasa, and Damodara Pandita ‘punished’ the Lord with words” (CC, Madhya 1.259) — and in the summary of the Antya-lila: the second chapter, he says, tells of “the lesson the Lord gave Chota Haridasa” (CC, Antya 20.105). Hence the title of the chapter itself: “The Lesson Taught by the Punishment of Sri Haridasa.”

Mahaprabhu's severity is neither cruelty nor worldly anger. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains in the “Anubhashya”: the Lord is an ocean of mercy, and He punished His devotees to show people what true devotion is, how high the Vaishnavas stand above the three modes of nature, and how far from pure Vaishnava dharma are the customs of the pseudo-Vaishnavas to come. Madhavi-devi was a maha-bhagavata, and for the Lord's associate to accept rice from her was not forbidden; there is no fault in her at all, and in Haridasa's request there was not a shadow of worldly feeling. But the Lord foresaw that deceivers, citing such an example, would pass off prakrita-sahajiya as Vaishnava dharma. Therefore He, the teacher of the world, enacted the pastime of a beloved associate's severe punishment and, knowing the weakness of the souls of the age of Kali, gave so harsh an order. In this severity lies His highest mercy.

“In this pastime the Lord showed His compassion, taught the world renunciation and revealed the deep love of His own devotee. He showed the glory of the holy place, and He made His devotee His own. Through a single pastime the Lord accomplishes five or seven purposes.” (CC, Antya 2.168–169)

Following these verses and the “Anubhashya,” one of the biographies lists the fruits of this pastime: the Lord revealed His boundless mercy, taught how precious true renunciation is, showed how deeply His devotees are attached to Him, revealed the glory of the holy place, and accepted His devotees as His own. He also showed how faultless a Vaishnava's life and character must be, and how poisonous is the fruit of even the subtlest touch of worldly attachment: one who wishes to become His devotee must give up worldly enjoyment to the very last trace. Outwardly rejecting Haridasa to teach the people, the Lord nevertheless accepted the service — the kirtana — of this pure devotee.

The Junior Haridasa was a pure and supremely saintly devotee of Mahaprabhu. He sang for the Lord in this world, and he sang for Him after leaving his body, when no one but the Lord could hear him; and his very story became the lesson Mahaprabhu taught all who seek pure devotion.

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, remembers him too — by the very thing for which he is known:

“Haridasa, dear to Gaura, found worthy of His punishment! Punish me and destroy my offences.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 63)

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Srila Haridasa Thakura, the Namacharya; the Senior Haridasa (Bada Haridasa), the Lord's other singer; Haridasa Pandita, the servant of Govindadeva in Vrindavana; Dvija Haridasa (Haridasa Acharya); the Haridasa of the second kirtana group at the Ratha-yatra (CC, Madhya 13.39; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta suggests that this may be the Senior Haridasa); and the Haridasa of a pada about Navadvipa, a companion of Mukunda, Madhava and Vasu; and Laghu Haridasa, one of the devotees with whom Rupa Gosvami went to see Gopala at Mathura (CC, Madhya 18.52) — Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura stresses that he is a different person. The Haridasa about whom the Lord asks, “Where is Haridasa?” (CC, Antya 2.150), is he.
  2. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” writes that Haridasa had taken bhek, the renunciant's garb. One of the biographies calls him “a sannyasi of immature age” and renders the Lord's words thus: “Even My mind is not under My control — how then will a sannyasi of immature years keep his mind steady while conversing with a woman?” The original sources are silent about Haridasa's age, and in the “Charitamrita” the Lord says something else (Antya 2.124, see below); we follow the “Charitamrita.”
  3. The verse names the pair “Raktaka and Patraka” and the pair “Haridasa the Elder and Haridasa the Younger”; the Junior Haridasa is second in his pair, that is, Patraka. So they are matched also in the table in the edition of Govinda Dasa's “Karcha.”
  4. One of the biographies names the Junior Haridasa here outright; another does too, but in a quotation of the English translation of the “Charitamrita,” where the word “junior” was added by the translator; a third puts a question mark beside his name. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on Madhya 13.42 also writes: “perhaps the Junior Haridasa?” — whereas the Haridasa of the second group (13.39) he tentatively takes to be the Senior. The Bengali verse 13.42 has simply “Haridasa”; the identification remains a conjecture.
  5. One of the biographies speaks of “a little rice of the best quality,” another of “fine rice.” Another reading of verse 2.103, cited in the “Anubhashya,” names a variety of rice called aroya. One of the biographies says that Haridasa came to beg rice from Madhavi-devi “in Bhagavan Acharya's house” and fell into conversation with her there; according to the “Charitamrita” (Antya 2.103) the Acharya sent him to her, to where she lived.
  6. Ishana Nagara in the “Advaita-prakasha” (18.138–148), a late source we trust less, tells it differently: the singer Sri Haridasa, “like a Gandharva, the best of bhagavatas, whose life was given to Gaura,” exchanged rice collected as alms for Gaura's service for better rice from “Mother Sri Madhavi”; the Lord asked Haridasa himself about the rice and, hearing his answer, said: “You have destroyed the eternal dharma of the detached. Although Madhavi is a great and chaste woman… a pure devotee of Krishna, still she is a woman… Therefore I reject you.” Haridasa wept bitterly, bowed and went away, and then Advaita and the others set out for Gauda. According to the “Charitamrita,” Haridasa begged the rice at Bhagavan Acharya's request, and the Lord asked the Acharya about it, not Haridasa; Kaviraja says nothing of an exchange of rice or of Advaita's presence, while Ishana says not a word about Haridasa going to Prayaga. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  7. One of the biographies writes that it was Govinda who was bewildered and grieved, knowing how dear the Junior Haridasa was to the Lord and not understanding why the door was barred to him. In the “Charitamrita” (Antya 2.114) it is Haridasa himself who is grieved.
  8. According to one of the biographies he fasted even without water; the “Charitamrita” speaks simply of a fast.
  9. In one of the biographies the reference is given as “Bhagavatam 9.19.15”; the verse is 9.19.17. Another biography attributes to the Lord the words that for a renunciant, talk with a woman is more harmful than poison; they are not in the “Charitamrita” (Antya 2.117–120).
  10. The Bengali text has avesha: the Lord was seized with anger. This is no worldly anger but the sternness of the Lord instructing the world.
  11. The biographies add that the devotees went to Puri on learning that Haridasa had decided to leave his body unless he could see the Lord, and that the Lord, unwilling to disregard Puri's words, agreed to let Haridasa back (even into the Gambhira) while He Himself would leave. According to the “Charitamrita,” they went to Puri the day after the Lord's rebuke, the Lord did not forgive Haridasa, and Haridasa left Puri only a year later (Antya 2.128–146).
  12. The biographies also cite here the Lord's words “I cannot tolerate a breach of propriety,” with a reference to “Adi 4.166”; this is Antya 4.166, and the words were spoken to Sanatana on another occasion.
  13. One of the biographies writes that Haridasa went to Prayaga at night, “having lost hope,” and bowed to Mahaprabhu in absentia at the Triveni itself. According to the “Charitamrita,” he bowed to the Lord at the end of the night, before leaving Puri (Antya 2.146), and entered the Triveni with a resolve (sankalpa) to attain the Lord's feet (2.147) — not out of despair.
  14. One of the biographies puts this guess in the mouth of Govinda alone and calls the spirit a “brahma-daitya.” According to the “Charitamrita” (Antya 2.155–156), “Govinda and all the others together” guessed, and the spirit is called a brahma-rakshasa; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta specifies: all except Svarupa.
  15. One of the biographies renders Svarupa's words as though Haridasa had left his body “in Sri Kshetra,” that is, in Puri. The Bengali verse 2.158 says “death in a holy place” (kshetrera marana), that is, at Prayaga, where he had gone.
  16. The Gaudiya Math edition reads verse 2.166 prabhu-pasha aila, “came to the Lord”; another reading is prabhu-pada paila, “attained the Lord's feet.”
